studies.Population: 49,934 male health professionals in the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, aged 40–75 years at baseline
studies.Reference: Dietary glycemic index, glycemic load, insulin index, fiber and whole-grain intake in relation to risk of prostate cancer.
studies.Authors: Nimptsch K, Kenfield S, Jensen MK, Stampfer MJ, Franz M, Sampson L, Brand-Miller JC, Willett WC, Giovannucci E
studies.Timing: Dietary intake assessed from 1986 through 2002; incident prostate cancer followed through January 31, 2007
studies.comparison_type: Highest versus lowest quintile of whole-grain intake
studies.direction_imputation_reason: Comparison direction was not explicit; the protocol assumes high versus low exposure.

sample_size.excerpt: We investigated the association between dietary GI, GL, II, fiber, and whole grains and risk of total prostate cancer (n = 5,112) and subgroups of prostate cancer as defined by stage or grade in 49,934 male participants of the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

cases.excerpt: The recently developed insulin index (II) quantifies the postprandial insulin secretion, also taking into account these additional characteristics. We investigated the association between dietary GI, GL, II, fiber, and whole grains and risk of total prostate cancer (n = 5,112) and subgroups of prostate cancer as defined by stage or grade in 49,934 male participants of the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

effect_size.excerpt: Dietary GI, GL, II, or fiber was not associated with risk of total or subgroups of prostate cancer. We observed a positive association between dietary intake of whole grains and total prostate cancer (HR highest versus lowest quintile 1.13, 95% CI 1.03-1.24), which was attenuated after restriction to PSA-screened participants (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.17).

confidence_interval.excerpt: We observed a positive association between dietary intake of whole grains and total prostate cancer (HR highest versus lowest quintile 1.13, 95% CI 1.03-1.24), which was attenuated after restriction to PSA-screened participants (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.17).

p_value.excerpt: We observed a statistically significant positive association between whole-grain intake and risk of total prostate cancer (HR highest versus lowest quintile 1.13, 95% CI 1.03–1.24, p-trend=0.001) as well as for organ-confined, high-grade and low-grade prostate cancer, but not for advanced prostate cancer.
p_value.location: Table 2, whole grains section, total prostate cancer row

timing.excerpt: The study was initiated in 1986 when 51,529 US male health professionals (dentists, optometrists, osteopaths, podiatrists, pharmacists, veterinarians) aged between 40 and 75 years completed and returned a mailed health questionnaire ascertaining information on diet, anthropometric and lifestyle factors as well as medical history.

studies.Reference: Intake of whole-grain products and risk of prostate cancer among men in the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort study.
studies.Authors: Egeberg R, Olsen A, Christensen J, Johnsen NF, Loft S, Overvad K, Tjønneland A
studies.Timing: Diet was assessed at cohort participation, with a median follow-up of 12.4 years.
studies.comparison_type: per 50 g day(-1) higher total whole-grain product intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: provided information about diet and potential prostate cancer risk factors

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 26,691 men aged 50-64 years participated in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort study and provided information about diet and potential prostate cancer risk factors. During a median follow-up of 12.4 years, we identified 1,081 prostate cancer cases.

cases.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 12.4 years, we identified 1,081 prostate cancer cases.

effect_size.excerpt: Overall, there was no association between total intake of whole-grain products and prostate cancer risk (adjusted incidence rate ratio per 50 g day(-1): 1.00 (95% confidence interval: 0.96, 1.05)) as well as between intake of the specific whole-grain products: whole-grain rye bread, whole-grain bread, and oatmeal, and risk of prostate cancer. No risk estimates did differ according to either stage or grade of disease.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Overall, there was no association between total intake of whole-grain products and prostate cancer risk (adjusted incidence rate ratio per 50 g day(-1): 1.00 (95% confidence interval: 0.96, 1.05)) as well as between intake of the specific whole-grain products: whole-grain rye bread, whole-grain bread, and oatmeal, and risk of prostate cancer.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test was not performed because fewer than 10 studies were available. With a small number of studies, the test generally has insufficient power to reliably detect funnel plot asymmetry.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an effect size of 1.11 (95% CI: 0.97–1.26), indicating no statistically significant association between whole-grain intake and prostate cancer\aggressive. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 83.33%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
